title: Leveraging Deep Reinforcement Learning for Metacognitive Interventions across Intelligent Tutoring Systems
extended_summary: This paper asks whether adaptive metacognitive interventions delivered by deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can better support students’ preparation for future learning than a static classifier-based approach in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs). The focus is on helping students learn when and how to switch from a default forward-chaining strategy to a backward-chaining strategy in a logic tutor, and then transfer that skill to a later probability tutor that only supports backward chaining.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom-based comparative experiment with two consecutive studies, pre/post measures, control groups, and ANCOVA/repeated-measures analyses. It is not a randomized controlled trial fully reported as a single study with all credibility criteria, but the design is stronger than correlational evidence and provides credible causal inference signals.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced large effects on learning outcomes and transfer/future-learning performance, with several reported pairwise effects well above d=0.20 (e.g., d=0.88 to 2.5). Because benefits extended across both tutors and improved preparation for future learning, the practical impact is substantial.

interventions.use_case: adaptive metacognitive interventions embedded in two logic/probability tutors, using static classifier-based vs deep reinforcement learning-based policies to deliver nudges, direct presentation of backward-chaining strategy, or no intervention
random forest classification of students into metacognitive groups (Default, StrOnly, StrTime) from incoming competence/behavior features to drive static intervention assignment

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that DRL-based adaptive metacognitive interventions closed the gap between metacognitive groups and improved preparation for future learning across two ITSs. In Exp. 2 (n=112), the DRL groups significantly outperformed control peers on both logic and probability post-tests and normalized learning gain; for example, DefaultDRL exceeded DefaultCtrl by d=1.6 on logic post-test and d=2.5 on probability post-test, while StrOnlyDRL also significantly surpassed StrOnlyCtrl.
finding.measure: Metacognitive group performance, post-test scores, isomorphic post-test scores, and normalized learning gain (NLG) on logic and probability tutors; preparation for future learning via probability tutor performance after logic tutor intervention
finding.effect_size: d=1.6 to 2.5 (pairwise post-test comparisons reported); η2=0.61, 0.74
finding.std_deviation: reported means with SDs in tables; exact pooled SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The static RFC-based intervention improved only a subset of students. In Exp. 1 (n=121), StrOnlyRFC significantly outperformed control and caught up with StrTime on both tutors, but DefaultRFC did not differ meaningfully from control peers and did not show the broad benefits seen with DRL.
finding.measure: Post-test scores, isomorphic post-test scores, and NLG on logic and probability tutors
finding.std_deviation: reported means with SDs in tables; exact pooled SD not_reported
